scenario.description: An employee-relations manager must decide how to respond after Rowan missed two project deadlines and finalize the record, workload, support, and review plan.

shared_context.S1: Rowan missed two deadlines on the Atlas project during the past month.
shared_context.S2: Nina has proposed a formal performance-improvement plan, while Rowan's performance response is not yet finalized.
shared_context.S3: Maya has authority to determine the formal employee-relations response and its follow-up requirements.
shared_context.S4: Before closing an employee-relations review, Maya's normal practice is to hold a recorded round-robin check-in in which the employee, project lead, HR partner, and line manager each give their relevant firsthand statement before Maya decides.
shared_context.S5: When Maya selects an alternative response instead of a formal performance-improvement plan, the case record separately confirms whether that selected response complies with policy; deferring a plan does not by itself make the selected alternative noncompliant.

PF1.text: Rowan told Maya's coordinator that a migraine flare-up contributed to both missed deadlines and that Rowan can reliably work 32 hours per week for the next six weeks; Rowan wants the record to describe a temporary capacity limitation without naming the medical condition, but this has not reached Maya's case file.

PF2.text: Leah personally observed Nina change the Atlas priorities three times after Rowan had begun each deliverable, including two changes within 48 hours of the missed deadlines; Leah has not entered those observations in the employee-relations record.

PF3.text: Derek confirmed this week that a formal performance-improvement plan requires documented coaching on the same performance issue first, and no such coaching is documented for Rowan; he has not yet added the policy confirmation to Maya's review packet.

PF4.text: Nina verbally promised Rowan that, if the response focused on rebuilding the work process, she would hold one 30-minute one-to-one every Tuesday for six consecutive weeks; the promise remains outside the formal case notes.

acceptance_conditions: The response must be a supported reset rather than a formal performance-improvement plan.
The decision must explicitly mark a formal performance-improvement plan as impermissible because the required documented coaching is absent.
The record must identify the situation as involving both process disruption and a temporary capacity limitation.
Rowan's planned workload must be exactly 32 hours per week for the next six weeks.
The record must exclude the name of Rowan's medical condition.
Policy compliance for the selected supported response must be explicitly confirmed.
The settlement must include Nina's promised 30-minute Tuesday one-to-one structure for six consecutive weeks.

content_checks.C6: any(('one-to-one' in c['type'] or 'one_to_one' in c['type']) and c['target'] == 'Rowan' and c['minutes'] == 30 and c['weekday'] == 'Tuesday' and c['duration_weeks'] == 6 for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF2' in revealed and 'PF2' in credited_facts and 'PF2' in justification_fact_ids

decisive_facts.why: Rowan's stated temporary capacity fixes the workload at exactly 32 hours per week for the next six weeks and requires the record to omit the medical-condition name.
Leah's three priority-change observations change the finding to an explicit mixed process-and-capacity finding and must be cited as the supporting evidence.
The absence of documented prior coaching makes a formal performance-improvement plan impermissible and requires Maya to confirm that the selected supported response complies with policy.
Nina's prior promise changes the follow-up to exactly one 30-minute one-to-one every Tuesday for six consecutive weeks.
